**The two drivers eating into your stake**

The math breaks down cleanly into two sources of dilution:

1. **New investor money (~20pp impact).** The $4M in new money at a $16M pre-money valuation accounts for the dominant share of dilution. This is the standard cost of a priced round — investors are buying roughly 20% of the post-money company ($4M / $20M post), and the founders absorb most of that alongside the pool.

2. **Convertible note conversion (~5pp impact).** Your convertible note is converting in this round, and those conversion shares are coming from the same cap table. Notes that convert at a discount to the round price convert into more shares than their face value would suggest — which means more dilution for existing holders. Per the YC SAFE primer and standard convertible-note mechanics, note conversion dilution is borne by ALL pre-round holders on a pro-rata basis, including the founders. Confirm the conversion price (cap- or discount-driven) with your counsel before signing the round documents, since that drives exactly how many shares the noteholder receives.

**Your ownership story in one sentence:** a Series A at $16M pre-money / $4M new money drops the founders' collective stake from 83.3% to 62.5% — a loss of roughly 20.8 percentage points.

That is a meaningful move, and it comes from two separate forces pulling in the same direction.

**The two drivers eating into your stake**

The math breaks down cleanly into two sources of dilution:

1. **New investor money (~20pp impact).** The $4M in new money at a $16M pre-money valuation accounts for the dominant share of dilution. This is the standard cost of a priced round — investors are buying roughly 20% of the post-money company ($4M / $20M post), and the founders absorb most of that alongside the pool.

2. **Convertible note conversion (~5pp impact).** Your convertible note is converting in this round, and those conversion shares are coming from the same cap table. Notes that convert at a discount to the round price convert into more shares than their face value would suggest — which means more dilution for existing holders. Per the YC SAFE primer and standard convertible-note mechanics, note conversion dilution is borne by ALL pre-round holders on a pro-rata basis, including the founders. Confirm the conversion price (cap- or discount-driven) with your counsel before signing the round documents, since that drives exactly how many shares the noteholder receives.

One thing worth noting: the model shows **no option pool top-up** in this scenario. That keeps the numbers here clean, but if the term sheet requires expanding the option pool to 10–15% as part of the round, you will absorb that dilution in addition to what is shown — typically on a pre-money basis (i.e., before new-money shares are counted), which means the founders take the full pool hit. Ask the lead investor explicitly whether a pool top-up is expected at close, and at what percentage.

## Coaching Commentary

**Your ownership story in one sentence:** a Series A at $16M pre-money / $4M new money drops the founders' collective stake from 83.3% to 62.5% — a loss of roughly 20.8 percentage points.

That is a meaningful move, and it comes from two separate forces pulling in the same direction.

---

**The two drivers eating into your stake**

The math breaks down cleanly into two sources of dilution:

1. **New investor money (~20pp impact).** The $4M in new money at a $16M pre-money valuation accounts for the dominant share of dilution. This is the standard cost of a priced round — investors are buying roughly 20% of the post-money company ($4M / $20M post), and the founders absorb most of that alongside the pool.

2. **Convertible note conversion (~5pp impact).** Your convertible note is converting in this round, and those conversion shares are coming from the same cap table. Notes that convert at a discount to the round price convert into more shares than their face value would suggest — which means more dilution for existing holders. Per the YC SAFE primer and standard convertible-note mechanics, note conversion dilution is borne by ALL pre-round holders on a pro-rata basis, including the founders. Confirm the conversion price (cap- or discount-driven) with your counsel before signing the round documents, since that drives exactly how many shares the noteholder receives.

One thing worth noting: the model shows **no option pool top-up** in this scenario. That keeps the numbers here clean, but if the term sheet requires expanding the option pool to 10–15% as part of the round, you will absorb that dilution in addition to what is shown — typically on a pre-money basis (i.e., before new-money shares are counted), which means the founders take the full pool hit. Ask the lead investor explicitly whether a pool top-up is expected at close, and at what percentage.

---

**What the math does NOT show here**

The preferred investor ownership reads 0% in this scenario. That is a modeling artifact: this run modeled the priced round from the founders' perspective to show dilution, but the preferred series percentage will appear in the report's post-financing table with the full breakdown. Review that table to see exactly how the cap table sits after the round closes.

---

**One counsel review item**

There is one flagged item that requires a conversation with counsel before you finalize this round:

- **QSBS eligibility (IRC §1202, rule `delaware_cross_border.qsbs_date_sensitive`).** Whether your common shares qualify for the Qualified Small Business Stock gain exclusion depends on issuance date, aggregate gross assets at issuance, active business requirements, and the specific OBBBA timing rules. Post-OBBBA (Public Law 119-21), the rules governing stock acquired after July 4, 2025 differ from prior law. This is not a determination this analysis can make — it requires counsel to review the issuance dates and the company's status at each grant. The upside is real (up to 100% federal gain exclusion on qualifying shares held for 5+ years), so it is worth the conversation.

This is the only counsel item flagged in this run, and it is a tax-planning item rather than a deal-structure red flag.
